source_refs.note: Topic printed as 5.3, printed pages 161-163: the mechanism and disadvantages of photorespiration, C-4 photosynthesis and CAM metabolism.

blocks.text: The respiratory activity that occurs in green cells in the presence of light, resulting in the release of carbon dioxide, is photorespiration. It needs oxygen and produces CO2 and H2O like aerobic respiration, but no ATP is produced.

blocks.title: Recalling
blocks.text: During carbon fixation rubisco combines three molecules of CO2 with three molecules of RuBP and makes six molecules of 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA).

RuBP carboxylase (rubisco) catalyses the addition of CO2 to RuBP to make phosphoglyceric acid (phosphoglycerate), which is further reduced to form glucose. But when the relative concentration of CO2 decreases and there is more oxygen in the leaf cells, rubisco adds O2 to RuBP instead of CO2. RuBP then breaks into two molecules, one phosphoglycerate and one phosphoglycolate (a two-carbon molecule).

Phosphoglycolate is converted into glycolate, which moves from the chloroplast to a peroxisome. There it is metabolised to glyoxylate using O2, a reaction that also produces toxic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Glyoxylate is converted to glycine, which is transported to a mitochondrion, where two molecules of glycine form one molecule of serine. Serine is transported to the peroxisome and converted to glycerate; glycerate moves to the chloroplast, where it is changed to phosphoglycerate, which can re-enter the Calvin cycle.

blocks.alt: Three organelles side by side. In the chloroplast rubisco adds oxygen to RuBP, giving phosphoglycerate and phosphoglycolate; the latter becomes glycolate and passes to the peroxisome, where it becomes glyoxylate (making hydrogen peroxide) and glycine. In the mitochondrion two glycine make serine, releasing carbon dioxide. Serine returns to the peroxisome as glycerate and then to the chloroplast as phosphoglycerate.
blocks.caption: The reactions of photorespiration across the chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion (original diagram after Figure 5.21 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: When oxygen is high and carbon dioxide low, rubisco adds O2 to RuBP instead of CO2, splitting it into phosphoglycerate, which re-enters the Calvin cycle, and the two-carbon phosphoglycolate. Phosphoglycolate becomes glycolate, which the peroxisome oxidises to glyoxylate, producing toxic hydrogen peroxide, and then glycine. In the mitochondrion two glycines form one serine and release CO2. Serine goes back to the peroxisome to become glycerate, then to the chloroplast as phosphoglycerate. Oxygen is consumed and CO2 released, but no ATP is made.

blocks.text: Plants that use the Calvin cycle to fix carbon are C-3 plants. When photorespiration occurs in them, they lose between 25 and 50 percent of their fixed carbon, which reduces their yields. The rate of photorespiration also depends on temperature: at higher temperatures the oxidative activity of rubisco increases more than its carbon-fixing activity. In tropical climates, especially where the temperature is often above 28 degrees Celsius, the problem is severe and has a major negative impact on agricultural yields.

blocks.title: How the problem arose
blocks.text: When photosynthesis first evolved there was little oxygen in the atmosphere, so there was little or no photorespiration. After millions of years free O2 accumulated in the atmosphere and competition started between CO2 and O2 for the same active site of rubisco. That led to the problem photorespiration now poses.
Adaptations to the problem of photorespiration
Plants of warmer climates evolved two ways to deal with photorespiration: C-4 photosynthesis and CAM metabolism. C-4 and CAM plants carry out C-4 as well as C-3 photosynthesis.

Some plants, including the grasses corn, sugarcane and sorghum and about two dozen other plant groups, run a special pathway called C-4 photosynthesis in addition to the normal Calvin cycle. In their leaves the mesophyll cells have fewer air spaces, and the enzymes of the Calvin cycle are deposited mainly in specialised bundle-sheath cells, which are impermeable to CO2.

In C-4 photosynthesis, in the mesophyll cells, CO2 is attached to the three-carbon molecule phosphoenol pyruvic acid, forming the four-carbon oxaloacetic acid; because this first product has four carbons the process is called C-4 photosynthesis and the plants C-4 plants. Oxaloacetic acid is converted to malic acid using NADH, and malic acid is transported to an adjacent bundle-sheath cell, where it is broken down to pyruvic acid and CO2. These cells can hold CO2, so its concentration rises and they run the Calvin cycle instead of photorespiration. The pyruvic acid returns to the mesophyll cell and is converted again to phosphoenol pyruvic acid using an ATP.

blocks.title: The cost of C-4
blocks.text: In C-4 photosynthesis the energy cost of making a glucose molecule is almost double. But in hot climates, where photorespiration would otherwise remove more than half the carbon fixed, it is the best compromise available.

blocks.alt: Left, C-3 photosynthesis: in a mesophyll cell CO2 joins RuBP and the Calvin cycle makes sugar. Right, C-4 photosynthesis: in the mesophyll cell CO2 joins PEP to make oxaloacetic acid and then malic acid, which passes into a bundle-sheath cell and releases CO2 for the Calvin cycle there; pyruvic acid returns and ATP remakes PEP.
blocks.caption: C-3 photosynthesis compared with C-4 photosynthesis (original diagram after Figure 5.22 of the chapter).
blocks.long_description: In a C-3 plant rubisco in the mesophyll fixes CO2 directly onto RuBP, and when CO2 is low and O2 high it photorespires instead. In a C-4 plant the mesophyll cell first attaches CO2 to phosphoenol pyruvic acid, giving four-carbon oxaloacetic acid, which NADH reduces to malic acid; malic acid moves into the bundle-sheath cell and releases CO2 there, so rubisco meets a high CO2 concentration and runs the Calvin cycle; the pyruvic acid goes back and an ATP turns it into PEP again.

blocks.text: In hot climates many succulent plants such as cacti, pineapples and some other plant groups perform crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, named after the plant family Crassulaceae in which it was first discovered. In these plants the stomata open during the night and close during the day. Closing the stomata by day prevents the loss of water and the removal of CO2, so the rate of photorespiration is reduced by the high concentration of carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide needed to make sugar is provided from organic molecules made the night before. Like C-4 plants, these plants use both the C-4 and the C-3 pathways.

blocks.prompt: Why does photorespiration get worse on a hot afternoon, and how do corn and cacti each avoid it?
blocks.explanation: At high temperatures rubisco's oxidative activity rises faster than its carbon-fixing activity, and stomata close to save water so CO2 falls while O2 builds up; rubisco then adds O2 to RuBP. Corn, a C-4 plant, fixes CO2 onto PEP in the mesophyll and delivers it as malic acid to bundle-sheath cells, where the high CO2 keeps rubisco on the Calvin cycle. Cacti, CAM plants, open their stomata only at night, store CO2 in organic acids, and release it to the Calvin cycle by day behind closed stomata.

items: Photorespiration: in light, with high O2 and low CO2, rubisco adds O2 to RuBP, giving phosphoglycerate and phosphoglycolate; the glycolate path through peroxisome (H2O2) and mitochondrion (two glycines to serine, CO2 released) returns glycerate to the chloroplast. O2 used, CO2 released, no ATP.
C-3 plants lose 25 to 50 percent of fixed carbon, worse above 28 degrees Celsius; the problem arose as atmospheric O2 accumulated and competed with CO2 for rubisco's active site.

C-4 plants (corn, sugarcane, sorghum) fix CO2 onto PEP in the mesophyll (oxaloacetic to malic acid) and release it in CO2-tight bundle-sheath cells for the Calvin cycle, at nearly double the energy cost. CAM plants (cacti, pineapple) open stomata at night, store CO2 in organic acids and use it by day.
